P0500.d: The vehicle speed signal A comes, depending on the maker, from a sensor on the gearbox, the transmission output speed, the wheel speeds via ABS/ESP or a CAN message; CARB explicitly names it as an input to be monitored. P0500 is the general code for this signal.
c: ABS/ESP module or wheel speed sensor faulty (signal source)
Output speed sensor or vehicle speed sensor faulty or dirty (metal debris on the magnet)
Wire or connector open or shorted, corrosion
Wrong tyre or axle data programmed

P0501.d: The vehicle speed signal A comes, depending on the maker, from a sensor on the gearbox, the transmission output speed, the wheel speeds via ABS/ESP or a CAN message; CARB explicitly names it as an input to be monitored. P0501 means the signal is present but does not fit the driving state or lies outside the physically possible range.
c: Wheel speed sensor or tone ring damaged or dirty (ABS source)
Wrong tyre size, axle ratio or coding
Sensor with weak signal or damaged tone wheel
Interference from damaged shielding or ground

P0502.d: The vehicle speed signal A comes, depending on the maker, from a sensor on the gearbox, the transmission output speed, the wheel speeds via ABS/ESP or a CAN message; CARB explicitly names it as an input to be monitored. Despite its wording, all makers found check plausibility: the car is clearly moving (load, torque, overrun), yet the signal stays at zero.
c: Speed or output speed sensor faulty
Wire open or shorted to ground, connector corroded
ABS module sends no speed signal
Tone wheel damaged or sensor dirty

P0503.d: The vehicle speed signal A comes, depending on the maker, from a sensor on the gearbox, the transmission output speed, the wheel speeds via ABS/ESP or a CAN message; CARB explicitly names it as an input to be monitored. P0503 combines three fault patterns: sporadic signal loss, jumping values and a value that is too high.
s: Cruise control drops out, jerky shifting
c: Loose contact, chafed wire, corroded connector
Interference from damaged shielding or the ignition
Sensor with weakened magnet or damaged tone wheel

P0504.d: The brake pedal switch has two contacts – A usually for the brake lights, B for cruise control and brake information – working in opposite sense, so the module expects opposite states on every brake application. P0504 means they disagree.
s: Cruise control cannot be switched on
Brake lights stay on or do not come on
Selector lever cannot be moved out of P
c: Brake light switch faulty (burnt or corroded contact)
Switch misadjusted or retaining clip or stop pad worn
Wire, connector or brake light fuse faulty
Moisture in fuse or junction boxes

P0505.d: CARB requires the idle speed control to be monitored: petrol engines must flag a fault if the target idle speed is not reached within +200/−100 rpm, diesels within ±30 %. Older engines use a separate idle air control valve that bypasses the closed throttle; with electronic throttle the throttle itself controls idle and no separate valve exists.
s: Idle speed fluctuates, too high or too low
Engine stalls at idle or when coasting
c: Throttle body or idle valve dirty or gummed
False air (hoses, intake gasket, crankcase ventilation)
Idle valve faulty mechanically or electrically
Learned values not reset after cleaning

P0506.d: CARB requires the idle speed control to be monitored: petrol engines must flag a fault if the target idle speed is not reached within +200/−100 rpm, diesels within ±30 %. Older engines use a separate idle air control valve that bypasses the closed throttle; with electronic throttle the throttle itself controls idle and no separate valve exists.
s: Engine stalls when stopping or with A/C on
Check engine light after two trips
c: Deposits at the throttle or bypass channel, or gummed idle valve
Extra load: stiff accessory drive, gearbox or converter
Intake or exhaust restricted (air filter, catalyst)
Idle valve or throttle actuator faulty, wrong learned value

P0507.d: CARB requires the idle speed control to be monitored: petrol engines must flag a fault if the target idle speed is not reached within +200/−100 rpm, diesels within ±30 %. Older engines use a separate idle air control valve that bypasses the closed throttle; with electronic throttle the throttle itself controls idle and no separate valve exists.
c: False air (vacuum hose, intake gasket, brake booster)
Crankcase ventilation leaking or wrongly routed
Throttle not closing fully (deposits, ice, stop misadjusted)
Wrong throttle learned value after cleaning or replacement

Older engines use a separate idle air control valve that bypasses the closed throttle; with electronic throttle the throttle itself controls idle and no separate valve exists.
s: Check engine light on at once
c: Control wire shorted to ground or open
Connector contact at valve or module

P0509.d: CARB requires the idle speed control to be monitored: petrol engines must flag a fault if the target idle speed is not reached within +200/−100 rpm, diesels within ±30 %. Older engines use a separate idle air control valve that bypasses the closed throttle; with electronic throttle the throttle itself controls idle and no separate valve exists.
s: Check engine light on at once

P050A.d: After a cold start the engine module raises idle speed and air mass and retards the ignition so that much heat goes into the exhaust and the catalyst lights off quickly. CARB requires this cold-start strategy to be monitored with its own codes, separate from ordinary idle and ignition faults.
s: Idle after a cold start too low, too high or hunting
Occasional stalling shortly after a cold start
c: Throttle or idle valve dirty or coked, not enough air when cold
Fault in the throttle or idle valve circuit
Extra load at cold start (alternator, A/C), stiff engine

P050B.d: After a cold start the engine module raises idle speed and air mass and retards the ignition so that much heat goes into the exhaust and the catalyst lights off quickly. CARB requires this cold-start strategy to be monitored with its own codes, separate from ordinary idle and ignition faults.
s: Catalyst warms up more slowly after a cold start
c: Idle control takes back the retard because speed would drop (false air, dirty throttle)
Knock control or knock sensor intervenes
Extra load or alternator at cold start

P050C.d: P050C is documented only on Bosch ME9 in the Saab 9-3 V6 2.8 turbo: a cold-start plausibility check of the coolant temperature sensor. After a long stop coolant and intake air must read about the same; the code sets if coolant is more than 10 °C below or 15 °C above intake air, once per trip with the warning lamp.
s: Rough running after a cold start
Radiator fan runs with a cold engine
c: Coolant temperature sensor drifting, wrong characteristic
Contact resistance or corrosion at the coolant or intake air sensor connector
Intake air temperature sensor reading wrong
Auxiliary heater or block heater not recognised, very short stop

P050D.d: GM's direct-injection petrol engines (from about 2016) split the injection into two pulses and retard the ignition after a cold start to heat the catalyst. P050D counts engine cycles with incomplete combustion via the crankshaft misfire detection during this strategy; if the rate reaches the catalyst-damaging misfire threshold, the code sets – once per trip, while the strategy is active (under 45 s running, coolant u
s: Check engine light on (depending on calibration)
Rough idle or jerking in the first seconds after a cold start
c: Injector with poor spray pattern or deposits, or injector circuit fault
Spark plug or ignition coil weak
Poor fuel or low fuel pressure

P050E.d: After a cold start the engine module raises idle speed and air mass and retards the ignition so that much heat goes into the exhaust and the catalyst lights off quickly. CARB requires this cold-start strategy to be monitored with its own codes, separate from ordinary idle and ignition faults.
c: Idle or air control does not reach the cold-start target (dirty throttle, false air)
Ignition not retarded enough (knock or torque intervention)

P050F.d: GM (from about model year 2017/18) monitors the brake booster with a vacuum sensor: with the pedal at rest and high intake vacuum the booster must hold its vacuum; a loss over time is filtered as a drift ratio, and above a threshold P050F sets, MIL after two trips. It runs with the engine on, during start-stop auto-stops and after switch-off.
s: Hard brake pedal, especially after auto-stop
Hissing at the pedal, start-stop stops less often
c: Leaking vacuum hose or check valve
Leaking diaphragm in the brake booster
Vacuum sensor or its seal faulty
Electric or mechanical vacuum pump weak (where fitted)

P0510.d: Older engines with a mechanical throttle have a separate idle contact on the throttle or the combined throttle position sensor (Bosch Motronic throttle switch, Nissan and Toyota sensors with idle switch). The module uses it to recognise idle – for idle control, fuel cut-off on overrun and idle ignition timing – and as a substitute if the position sensor fails.
s: No fuel cut-off on overrun (higher consumption)
c: Idle switch or throttle sensor misadjusted
Switch contacts worn, dirty or corroded
Wire or connector open or shorted
Throttle not closing (deposits, sticking cable, stop misadjusted)

P0511.d: CARB requires the idle speed control to be monitored: petrol engines must flag a fault if the target idle speed is not reached within +200/−100 rpm, diesels within ±30 %. Older engines use a separate idle air control valve that bypasses the closed throttle; with electronic throttle the throttle itself controls idle and no separate valve exists.
s: Idle too high, too low or fluctuating
c: Idle valve faulty (coil open or shorted)

P0512.d: The engine module reads a start request – from the ignition switch, a start button via the body module, or start-stop – and drives the starter relay with it. P0512 flags a fault in this signal.
s: Engine does not start, starter does not crank
Starter keeps running after the start (noise)
Check engine light (Subaru after two trips)
c: Ignition or start switch, or start button, faulty or sticking
Harness chafed, short to ground or positive
Selector or clutch switch in the start path

P0513.d: The engine module receives a secret code from the immobiliser or body module (Chrysler SKIM/SKREEM/RF hub, Saab CIM); if it does not match the stored code, P0513 sets and starting is prevented – Saab cuts fuel and blocks the starter. The most common trigger is a replaced or reflashed engine module that was not taught to the immobiliser (FCA, Saab), less often handshake timing on FCA hybrids or a key not programmed.
s: Engine does not start or stops after 1–2 s
c: Engine module replaced or reflashed and not taught to the immobiliser
Key or transponder not programmed or faulty
Immobiliser, body or RF hub module replaced or faulty

P0514.d: The battery temperature sensor – usually an NTC in the battery tray or inside an intelligent battery sensor on the negative terminal – lets the module adjust the charging voltage (higher when cold, lower when warm) and supports battery management and start-stop. P0514 is the plausibility check of the temperature signal.
s: Charging voltage too high or too low
c: Corrosion at sensor or connector near the battery acid
Sensor fitted wrongly after a battery change

P0515.d: The battery temperature sensor – usually an NTC in the battery tray or inside an intelligent battery sensor on the negative terminal – lets the module adjust the charging voltage (higher when cold, lower when warm) and supports battery management and start-stop. P0515 is its general circuit fault – open or short – without separating low and high; the charging voltage is then fixed or conservative.
c: Sensor not plugged in after a battery change

P0516.d: The battery temperature sensor – usually an NTC in the battery tray or inside an intelligent battery sensor on the negative terminal – lets the module adjust the charging voltage (higher when cold, lower when warm) and supports battery management and start-stop. P0516 means the signal voltage stays below its limit for a minimum time; with an NTC in a voltage divider a low voltage means very hot, or more often a signa
s: Battery weak, starting problems in the cold
c: Signal line shorted to ground (chafed at the battery tray)
Moisture or acid in the connector

P0517.d: The battery temperature sensor – usually an NTC in the battery tray or inside an intelligent battery sensor on the negative terminal – lets the module adjust the charging voltage (higher when cold, lower when warm) and supports battery management and start-stop. P0517 means the signal voltage is above its limit, close to the reference; with an NTC that means very cold, or more often an open circuit – sensor unplugged
c: Sensor unplugged or forgotten after a battery change
Wire or connector open or corroded

P0518.d: Older engines without electronic throttle have a separate idle air control valve bypassing the closed throttle; CARB requires its output to be checked but not the fault types to be coded separately. P0518 means its circuit fails sporadically – the signal or current briefly leaves its valid range and returns.
s: Engine stalls when coasting or stopping
Check engine light (depending on the maker)
c: Loose contact or corrosion at the idle valve connector
Broken or chafed wire in the harness

P0519.d: P0519 means the idle control fails functionally with an electrically sound circuit – the actual idle speed deviates strongly despite fully used control. It is documented only on Subaru (also in the Saab 9-2X, electronic throttle, around 2005): idle at least 1000 rpm above target with the control already at zero for 2 or 5 s sets the code with the warning lamp at once, and a fail-safe cuts fuel to cylinders to stop th
s: Idle far above target, engine races
Jerking from cylinder cut-off in limp mode
c: False air behind the throttle (intake, gasket, vacuum hose)
Throttle or idle valve stuck open (foreign body, coking)
Follow-on fault of other codes (sensors, pedal)

P051A.d: The crankcase pressure sensor measures pressure in the crankcase ventilation (PCV) against atmosphere; Ford's EcoBoost engines use it for the disconnection check P04DB, which needs a sound sensor. P051A is the sensor's general circuit fault.
c: Connector or supply, ground or SENT signal wire open or corroded
Oil or moisture in the connector

P051B.d: The crankcase pressure sensor measures pressure in the crankcase ventilation (PCV) against atmosphere; Ford's EcoBoost engines use it for the disconnection check P04DB, which needs a sound sensor. P051B is its plausibility check.
s: Possibly oil leaks or oil mist (real overpressure)
c: PCV or blow-by valve sticking, ventilation blocked or frozen (real overpressure)

P051C.d: The crankcase pressure sensor measures pressure in the crankcase ventilation (PCV) against atmosphere; Ford's EcoBoost engines use it for the disconnection check P04DB, which needs a sound sensor. P051C means the signal of the analogue ratiometric sensor is too low – Ford sets it below 0.44 V for 5 s.
c: 5 V reference or signal line open or shorted to ground
5 V reference pulled down by another sensor

P051D.d: The crankcase pressure sensor measures pressure in the crankcase ventilation (PCV) against atmosphere; Ford's EcoBoost engines use it for the disconnection check P04DB, which needs a sound sensor. P051D means the signal is too high – Ford sets it above 4.56 V for 5 s.

P051E.d: The crankcase pressure sensor measures pressure in the crankcase ventilation (PCV) against atmosphere; Ford's EcoBoost engines use it for the disconnection check P04DB, which needs a sound sensor. P051E means the signal jumps or briefly drops below or above its limits – physically impossible changes, usually from a loose contact.
c: Loose contact at the sensor connector
Oil or water in the connector

P051F.d: The crankcase ventilation has an oil mist separator or filter element that can clog; the crankcase pressure sensor then sees rising pressure at a given flow. P051F reports this restriction.
s: Oil leaks at seals or dipstick
Oil mist in the intake, higher oil consumption
c: Separator or filter clogged with oil, soot or sludge
Icing in the separator or hose on short winter trips

P0520.d: The oil pressure sensor matters for emissions control because modern engines use it as an input – for two-stage or regulated oil pumps, hydraulic cam phasers and GM's cylinder deactivation, whose lifters switch by oil pressure. P0520 is the general circuit fault, used differently: Ford petrol and diesel engines set it for the digital SENT sensor when it reports an internal fault, does not initialise or sends values o
s: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
Oil pressure gauge or warning wrong
Cam phasing or cylinder deactivation possibly disabled
c: Connector corroded or oily (oil creeping through a leaking sensor)
Signal line open or shorted to ground
5 V reference or supply faulty (usually with other sensor codes)

P0521.d: The oil pressure sensor matters for emissions control because modern engines use it as an input – for two-stage or regulated oil pumps, hydraulic cam phasers and GM's cylinder deactivation, whose lifters switch by oil pressure. P0521 is the plausibility check.
s: Oil pressure reading implausible or fluctuating
Cylinder deactivation or cam phasing possibly disabled
c: Oil pump control valve or two-stage pump stuck in the wrong stage
Wrong viscosity, low oil level or foaming oil

P0522.d: The oil pressure sensor matters for emissions control because modern engines use it as an input – for two-stage or regulated oil pumps, hydraulic cam phasers and GM's cylinder deactivation, whose lifters switch by oil pressure. P0522 means the signal voltage is below its limit: GM 2018 below 5 % of the 5 V reference, Ford petrol below 0.25 V, Ford diesel below 0.018 V, about 5 s.
s: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
Oil pressure gauge at zero or warning despite normal pressure
Cam phasing or cylinder deactivation possibly disabled
c: Signal line shorted to ground or open

P0523.d: The oil pressure sensor matters for emissions control because modern engines use it as an input – for two-stage or regulated oil pumps, hydraulic cam phasers and GM's cylinder deactivation, whose lifters switch by oil pressure. P0523 means the signal voltage is above its limit: GM 2018 above 95 % of the 5 V reference, GM 2006 above 4.89 V, Ford petrol above 4.75 V, Ford diesel above 4.992 V, about 5 s.
s: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
Cam phasing or cylinder deactivation possibly restricted
c: Signal shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Oil or moisture in the connector

P0524.d: P0524 is not a sensor fault but a condition: the measured oil pressure is below a minimum depending on speed, load and temperature (Ford diesel 30–90 kPa) for about 5 s, with the sensor itself plausible. Its purpose is engine protection; Ford petrol engines with mid-lock cam phasers drive them into the locked position.
s: Oil pressure warning and/or check engine light
c: Oil level too low, oil loss or consumption
Too thin oil, fuel dilution or clogged pick-up screen
Oil pump or pressure control valve faulty or stuck
False setting by software in the cold (Ram EcoDiesel)

P0525.d: P0525 concerns vehicles with a separate cruise control servo – a vacuum or electric actuator on the throttle cable driven by the engine module: the control circuit is electrically sound, but the response does not match the command. With electronic throttle the engine module controls the throttle itself, so the code hardly applies there.
s: Cruise control inoperative or switches off
c: Servo worn or sticking, cable misadjusted
Vacuum leak at hose or diaphragm (vacuum servo)
Wiring, connector or fuse to the servo
Brake or clutch switch interrupting the servo release

P0526.d: Engine-driven fans with an electronically controlled viscous clutch (GM petrol SUVs and pick-ups 2004–2006, GM Duramax, Ford 6.7 L Power Stroke) have a Hall sensor reporting fan speed; the fan checks P0483, P0494 and P0495 need it. P0526 means no usable signal although the clutch is driven: GM Duramax below 500 rpm with fan duty at least 36 % for 2 s; the 6.6 L LML distinguishes a level stuck low or high; GM petrol V
s: Fan permanently on or off, loud fan noise
Weak air conditioning at low speed, overheating under load
c: Hall sensor at the fan clutch faulty
Wiring or connector (chafing at the shroud, corrosion)

P0527.d: Engine-driven fans with an electronically controlled viscous clutch (GM petrol SUVs and pick-ups 2004–2006, GM Duramax, Ford 6.7 L Power Stroke) have a Hall sensor reporting fan speed; the fan checks P0483, P0494 and P0495 need it. P0527 means a signal is present but implausible – spikes, jumps or a speed that does not fit the clutch command and engine speed.
s: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
c: Sensor or trigger element damaged, wrong air gap
Interference or ground fault on the sensor line
Viscous clutch slipping or sticking (real speed off)

P0528.d: Engine-driven fans with an electronically controlled viscous clutch (GM petrol SUVs and pick-ups 2004–2006, GM Duramax, Ford 6.7 L Power Stroke) have a Hall sensor reporting fan speed; the fan checks P0483, P0494 and P0495 need it. P0528 means no pulses arrive from the sensor although the fan should be turning.
s: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
Fan permanently on or not at all
c: Fan or clutch really not turning

P0529.d: Engine-driven fans with an electronically controlled viscous clutch (GM petrol SUVs and pick-ups 2004–2006, GM Duramax, Ford 6.7 L Power Stroke) have a Hall sensor reporting fan speed; the fan checks P0483, P0494 and P0495 need it. P0529 means the speed signal drops out or jumps at times.
s: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
Fan running permanently or not at all
c: Loose contact at connector or wiring at the fan (vibration, chafing)
Sensor in the fan clutch intermittently faulty

c: Cam phaser sticking or lock pin not releasing
Low oil level, wrong viscosity or sludged oil
Oil control valve sticking or screen clogged

P052E.d: P052E is a function fault of the crankcase ventilation pressure regulating valve. Audi's 3.0 TFSI has a diaphragm valve whose torn diaphragm or elbow causes false air and whistling; Mercedes' M270/M274 have a switched part-load ventilation valve that blocks with oil carbon and lets oil into the intake – blue smoke, rough running, lack of power; Mercedes extended the emission warranty on the intake module.
s: Whistling or hissing in the engine bay
Rough idle, blue smoke or oil consumption, lack of power
c: Diaphragm of the regulating valve torn or fatigued
Part-load ventilation valve blocked (oil carbon, sludge)
Elbow or hose at the valve cracked, clamp leaking

P052F.d: Diesel glow plugs are switched by a separate glow plug control module fed from the battery, with its own ground, a command from the engine module and a diagnostic line back. P052F means its supply voltage is out of range.
s: Hard cold start, long cranking, white smoke
Several glow plug codes at once
c: Main feed to the module open or high-resistance (fuse, connector, corroded ring terminal)
Poor ground of the glow plug module
System voltage too low or too high (weak battery, regulator fault)

P0530.d: The engine module reads the high-side refrigerant pressure sensor (5 V reference, signal rising with pressure) to switch or regulate the compressor, raise the radiator fans at high pressure and pre-control the compressor load at idle. CARB therefore requires A/C components to be monitored where they alter fuel or ignition control or feed other diagnoses (from 2006–2008).
s: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
c: Connector or contacts corroded or loose
5 V reference shorted by another sensor

P0531.d: The engine module reads the high-side refrigerant pressure sensor (5 V reference, signal rising with pressure) to switch or regulate the compressor, raise the radiator fans at high pressure and pre-control the compressor load at idle. CARB therefore requires A/C components to be monitored where they alter fuel or ignition control or feed other diagnoses (from 2006–2008).
c: Refrigerant charge wrong (too little or too much)
Compressor or control valve delivering poorly

P0532.d: The engine module reads the high-side refrigerant pressure sensor (5 V reference, signal rising with pressure) to switch or regulate the compressor, raise the radiator fans at high pressure and pre-control the compressor load at idle. CARB therefore requires A/C components to be monitored where they alter fuel or ignition control or feed other diagnoses (from 2006–2008).
s: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
c: Signal line open or shorted to ground

P0533.d: The engine module reads the high-side refrigerant pressure sensor (5 V reference, signal rising with pressure) to switch or regulate the compressor, raise the radiator fans at high pressure and pre-control the compressor load at idle. CARB therefore requires A/C components to be monitored where they alter fuel or ignition control or feed other diagnoses (from 2006–2008).
s: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
c: Signal line shorted to positive (e.g. 5 V reference)
Extreme overpressure (overcharge, blocked condenser, fan off)

P0534.d: P0534 reports too little refrigerant (a leak), not a sensor circuit: the module compares pressure or temperature in the circuit with a model, and the compressor is locked out for protection. FCA's 2020 Ram EcoDiesel sets it with the warning lamp; a software update fixed false setting.
s: Air conditioning weak or not cooling
Check engine light or high-voltage service message (electric)
c: Refrigerant leak (condenser, joints, compressor shaft seal, service ports)
Traction battery chiller faulty (electric and hybrid only)

P0535.d: The evaporator temperature sensor, an NTC thermistor behind the evaporator, prevents icing: near 0–3 °C the compressor is switched off or reduced. Usually the climate module reads it and reports body codes; P0535–P0539 only arise where the engine module controls the compressor and reads the sensor.
s: Air conditioning not or weakly cooling

P0536.d: The evaporator temperature sensor, an NTC thermistor behind the evaporator, prevents icing: near 0–3 °C the compressor is switched off or reduced. Usually the climate module reads it and reports body codes; P0535–P0539 only arise where the engine module controls the compressor and reads the sensor.
c: Sensor not seated correctly in the evaporator

P0537.d: The evaporator temperature sensor, an NTC thermistor behind the evaporator, prevents icing: near 0–3 °C the compressor is switched off or reduced. Usually the climate module reads it and reports body codes; P0535–P0539 only arise where the engine module controls the compressor and reads the sensor.
s: Compressor permanently on or locked out
c: Condensate in the connector (leakage to ground)

P0538.d: The evaporator temperature sensor, an NTC thermistor behind the evaporator, prevents icing: near 0–3 °C the compressor is switched off or reduced. Usually the climate module reads it and reports body codes; P0535–P0539 only arise where the engine module controls the compressor and reads the sensor.
s: Air conditioning not cooling (compressor locked out)
c: Connector off or corroded, wire open

P0539.d: The evaporator temperature sensor, an NTC thermistor behind the evaporator, prevents icing: near 0–3 °C the compressor is switched off or reduced. Usually the climate module reads it and reports body codes; P0535–P0539 only arise where the engine module controls the compressor and reads the sensor.
c: Loose contact or corrosion at the connector
Broken wire from movement or chafing

P053A.d: The PCV heater is an electric element of a few ohms (Saab: 6–10 Ω) at the junction of the ventilation hose and the intake; it stops water in the blow-by gas from freezing and blocking the ventilation in frost. The module switches it to ground.
s: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
In frost: oil leaks or loss of power from frozen ventilation
c: Fuse of the ignition supply blown

P053B.d: The PCV heater is an electric element of a few ohms (Saab: 6–10 Ω) at the junction of the ventilation hose and the intake; it stops water in the blow-by gas from freezing and blocking the ventilation in frost. The module switches it to ground.
s: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
c: Heating element shorted to its housing

P053C.d: The PCV heater is an electric element of a few ohms (Saab: 6–10 Ω) at the junction of the ventilation hose and the intake; it stops water in the blow-by gas from freezing and blocking the ventilation in frost. The module switches it to ground.
s: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
In frost: oil leaks or loss of power from frozen ventilation
c: Heating element shorted internally (very low resistance, overcurrent)

P053D.d: The PCV heater is an electric element of a few ohms (Saab: 6–10 Ω) at the junction of the ventilation hose and the intake; it stops water in the blow-by gas from freezing and blocking the ventilation in frost. The module switches it to ground.
s: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
In frost: oil leaks or loss of power from frozen ventilation
c: Heating element aged (resistance outside 6–10 Ω, Saab reference)
Increased contact resistance at the connector
Partial short in the element (overcurrent, driver overheating)

P053E.d: P053E is the system code for crankcase pressure above an operating-point limit while the sensor itself is plausible. Normally the crankcase runs at a slight vacuum (GM: −1 to −5 inH2O).
s: Oil leaks at seals, dipstick pushed out
c: Ventilation or oil separator blocked or frozen
Pressure regulating or PCV valve faulty
Increased blow-by (piston rings, turbo oil side)
Leaking vacuum reservoir or pump in the valve cover

P053F.d: Petrol direct-injection engines often inject twice after a cold start, once late in the compression stroke, to heat the catalyst; this needs rail pressure within a window. P053F reports that the window was not reached often enough.

P05EB sets when the measured temperature at the SCR inlet stays below the expected or modelled value within a set time after the start: the heating strategy is not wor
s: Higher NOx emissions after cold start (not noticeable)
c: Engine module software or calibration (false trigger)

Heating measure not effective: throttle, EGR cooler bypass or turbo vanes sticking
Post or retarded injection not effective (injectors)
Exhaust leak before the sensor or extremely cold conditions

P05EC.d: To heat the exhaust after a cold start, a diesel shifts its start of injection, usually later, plus post injections. CARB requires faults of such elements during the cold start strategy to be reported under codes separate from normal operation – hence P05EC.
s: Possibly more white smoke or rougher running after cold start
c: Engine module software or internal fault (request and execution differ)
Cold start mode blocked by other faults (coolant or fuel temperature, rail pressure)

P05ED.d: Some diesels use a separate control module or power stage for the DEF heaters in tank, pump and lines; without heating, frozen fluid cannot thaw in winter and dosing stays blocked. P05ED reports that this module's supply voltage is outside its allowed window – a blown main fuse, an open feed or ground, or system voltage too low or too high.
s: DEF/AdBlue warning, possibly countdown to no-restart
In cold weather: DEF frozen, dosing blocked, further heater codes
c: Main fuse or feed wire to the heater module faulty, connector corroded (splash zone)
Weak battery or charging fault (system voltage too low or too high)

P05FB.d: A discrete stop-start status line tells the engine module (or another module) whether stop-start is active, inhibited or has just stopped the engine. On most current cars this status travels over CAN instead, so a hard-wired line and these codes are rare; no manufacturer document available to us uses P05F9–P05FB.
s: Stop-start indicator or message in the cluster
c: Open status line or connector off
Sending module faulty or without ground

P05FC.d: During a cold start, direct injection petrol engines usually raise rail pressure for finer atomisation with multiple injections while the catalyst heats up. P05FC monitors whether the actual rail pressure of bank 2 stays within the target window during this phase – only engines with separate rails and pressure sensors per bank (V or boxer engines with two high-pressure circuits) can set it.
s: Stumbling, hesitation or rough idle during warm-up
c: High-pressure pump or volume control valve of bank 2 weak or sticking
Rail pressure sensor of bank 2 inaccurate
Leaking injector or pressure relief on bank 2

P05FD.d: Electric variable-geometry turbo actuators use a DC motor with gearing, driven by an H-bridge in the engine module or in the actuator itself. Constant high load – sooted or stiff vanes, running against a stop, an internal motor short – drives up current and temperature.
s: Loss of power or limp mode
c: Vane mechanism sooted or stiff, actuator works constantly against resistance
Electric actuator faulty internally (shorted turns, bearing)
High ambient heat at the actuator (missing heat shield, exhaust leak)

P05FE.d: Active grille shutters close the air inlet when little cooling is needed, to reduce drag and speed up warm-up. P05FE is the performance check of a third shutter C – target and actual position do not match, as P059F does for shutter A and P05AE for shutter B.
s: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
Higher coolant temperature under load or slower warm-up
c: Debris or ice blocking the louvres

P05FF.d: Stop-start decides when to stop and restart the engine from the brake: Ford stops it when the pedal switch is on and master cylinder pressure is high enough, and restarts when pressure falls below a filtered reference. P05FF means brake pressure (from the sensor in the ABS unit, sent over the network) and brake pedal position do not agree – for example pedal pressed without pressure build-up, or pressure without peda
s: No check engine light at Ford, possibly wrench or service warning
Possible related codes P0504 or brake pressure codes
c: Brake pedal position sensor or switch misadjusted or faulty
Master cylinder pressure sensor in the ABS unit faulty
Network communication or software between ABS module and engine module
Air in the brake system or hydraulic fault (long pedal travel without pressure)
